No. 18· October 22, 2026· Global, Italy in focus· Illustrated edition
In three lines

The world

thedesk.net · October 15, 2026

Fox's AI agents start actually buying TV ad spots

Fox Advertising's AI-powered Fox AdStudio platform moved from demonstration to real transactions this week: WPP, Omnicom, Horizon Media, Stagwell and Simulmedia are now live on the agent-to-agent system, letting their systems and Fox's negotiate and complete linear TV ad buys automatically, without the phone calls, faxes, emails and spreadsheets a schedule normally takes. Fox first showed the capability in June 2026; this week is the first time it has handled real campaigns. Jeff Collins, president of Fox Advertising, called it "moving agentic advertising from capability to real-world execution while maintaining the governance and human oversight essential to doing it responsibly." Fox disclosed no transaction volumes or savings figures.

Why it mattersThe part of advertising that used to require a human on each end of a phone line just started running without one. What used to take days of back-and-forth now happens in milliseconds, and five of the industry's biggest buyers are already routing real money through it.
TheWrap / Tubefilter · October 14, 2026

TikTok signs its own Hollywood-style studio for creator-led microdrama

TikTok inked a multiyear deal with Made By Us Studios, described as a "Hollywood-grade studio designed for the creator economy," to co-produce a slate of vertical microseries exclusive to TikTok and its standalone drama app, PineDrama. The first two projects, unveiled at MIPCOM Cannes: "Player," a romantic revenge thriller starring and co-developed by creator Hannah Stocking, and "The Knock," a horror-genre series starring Adam Rose opposite Zaria Simone, directed by R.H. Stavis. The deal mirrors TikTok's earlier partnership with Issa Rae's HOORAE (see Content, below).

Why it mattersTikTok isn't just hosting creator content anymore, it's building the studio system around it, the same vertical integration a traditional network does when it stops licensing shows and starts producing them in-house.
nabshow.com / tvtechnology.com · opens October 21-22, 2026

NAB Show New York opens with the creator economy as its main draw

NAB Show New York returns to the Javits Center this week with more than 200 exhibitors, roughly 10% of them first-time participants, and about 80 hours of programming spanning AI, the creator economy, streaming, sports and broadcast. Last year's edition drew 11,500 registered attendees from 95 countries. Programming this year runs from brand-deal basics to equity partnerships and IP ownership, continuing a thread this brief has tracked since issue 12.

Why it mattersA trade show built for broadcast engineers now dedicates a large chunk of its floor to the people who film vertical video on their phones. That's the clearest sign yet of where the industry thinks the next decade of production actually happens.
beinsure.com / PYMNTS · status as of October 20, 2026

Google and the DOJ still haven't agreed on how fast the ad tech remedies happen

No change to report since issue 17: Judge Leonie Brinkema still hasn't signed the final order implementing her September ad tech ruling. The October 5 filing that set out competing versions (DOJ wants the AdX-Prebid integration live in 6 months and global rollout immediately; Google wants 12 months domestically plus 24 more before going global) remains unresolved two weeks later.

Why it matters"Google must open its ad exchange" sounded final a month ago. It still isn't binding on anyone until a judge picks a date, and that date is still missing.

Campaigns & brand moves

adsoftheworld.com / evenrealities.com · series launched October 8, 2026

Even Realities turns an ad campaign into an eight-episode cliffhanger series

Smart glasses brand Even Realities and agency VIRTUE Worldwide built "Exposed," an eight-episode cinematic microdrama directed by Ishana Night Shyamalan, around the tension of always-on camera glasses: a family in a near-future hotel discovers what happens to bystanders when every face becomes a lens. The series followed a September trailer and out-of-home placements in New York and San Francisco built around bystander privacy, before the full run started on TikTok on October 8.

Why it mattersEven Realities make camera-free smart glasses, so the whole campaign argues its own product category's risk before selling its alternative. Building that argument as a horror serial, not a manifesto, is what makes it land.
lvmh.com · October 16-18, 2026

LVMH opens 71 house venues across 13 countries, free, for one weekend

The sixth edition of Les Journées Particulières, running since 2011, opened 71 locations belonging to 45 LVMH maisons across 13 countries to the public this weekend under the theme "Aux Racines du Rêve" (At the Source of Dreams). Highlights included CELINE's Paris ready-to-wear workshops and Paris Match's archive room, both open to visitors for the first time, plus international venues like Casa Loewe in Madrid and Loro Piana's mill in Ulaanbaatar. LVMH paired the event with sustainability figures: 4.3 million hectares of natural habitat preserved or restored, and 99.9% of grapes from LVMH-owned vineyards under sustainable viticulture certification.

Why it mattersThe backstage, the vineyard, the workshop floor, the stuff a luxury house normally keeps closed, is the content here. No ad spend converts a craftsman's hands into brand trust as efficiently as watching them actually work.

What is working in content

TheWrap / Tubefilter · market data via essentiallypop.com / senalnews.com · October 14, 2026

The vertical microdrama keeps setting its own records

Issa Rae's HOORAE-produced "Screen Time" has passed 580 million views across TikTok and PineDrama since its April premiere, making it the top-performing show ever on either platform; it hit nearly 75 million views in its first week alone. That track record is why TikTok just signed a second studio deal (see News, above). The format's pull shows up in the market numbers too: global microdrama revenue is estimated to have grown from $11 billion in 2025 toward $14 billion by the end of 2026 (essentiallypop.com, citing industry trackers), inside a broader vertical-video economy outside China projected at $150 billion in 2026, up 41% year on year (senalnews.com). Flagged as industry estimates, not platform-disclosed figures.

Why it mattersA single TikTok series now outperforms most theatrical releases on raw view count, using a production budget a fraction of a streaming show's. The cliffhanger, not the production value, is doing the work, which is exactly why a brand (Even Realities, above) just borrowed the format outright.

  • October 9 report ("Make October magical with simple DIY ideas"): Pony Bead Tapestry Patterns +300%, Pumpkin Seed Recipes +100%, Easy Couple Halloween Costumes +100%, Monkey Bread Recipe +80%, Pumpkin Patch Outfits Women +60%.
  • October 16 report ("It's Cozy Season!"): Pumpkin Patch Hairstyles +100%, October Crafts for Kids +100%, Halloween Cookies +80%, Plaid Skirt Outfits Women +30%, October Fall Nails +100%.

Pinterest's search data keeps rewarding the specific, makeable thing over the generic seasonal category, the same "specificity beats vagueness" pattern this brief has tracked since issue 8.

The historical bridge

New York, 1914

The serial that invented the cliffhanger, on purpose

"The Perils of Pauline" premiered March 23, 1914 at Loew's Broadway Theatre, produced by William Randolph Hearst for Pathe's Eclectic Film Company. Pearl White played Pauline Marvin across 20 episodes released in bi-weekly installments, each one ending with the heroine in mortal danger, the device that gave English the word "cliffhanger" (partly from episodes filmed on the New Jersey Palisades, partly from the trope itself). Hearst ran a simultaneous serialized print version in his newspapers, and Pathe ran a $25,000 contest inviting fans to suggest plot points for Pauline's next peril.

Why it still holds. TikTok's PineDrama and the Made By Us Studios slate (above) are running the exact same playbook 112 years later: episodes engineered to end on a hook, a release cadence built to guarantee the audience comes back, and now, in TikTok's comment sections, the same crowd-sourced instinct Pathe paid $25,000 to manufacture in 1914. The format didn't need inventing. It needed a platform that could release a new episode every day instead of every two weeks.
